title: ANSI Grade 1 or EN 1125: Which Standard Your Exit Device Has to Meet
subtitle: Insight
text: ansi grade 1 or en 1125: which standard your exit device has to meet they are not two grades of the same thing. ansi/bhma a156.3 rates an exit device by cycles and force; en 1125 tests whether a panicking crowd can get out. which one you need is decided by the country your building is in, not by which sounds stronger. a buyer comparing exit devices across two catalogues will see "ansi grade 1" on one and "en 1125 certified" on the other and reasonably assume these are two ways of saying the same thing, one of which is better. they are not comparable at all. they are two regulatory worlds that test different properties for different reasons, and the question is never which is higher — it is which one the authority having jurisdiction over your building will accept. ansi/bhma a156.3 is the american standard for exit devices, and it grades them 1, 2 or 3 by durability. grade 1 is the heavy-duty tier: it survives the most operating cycles and the highest static and dynamic loads. the grade is fundamentally a statement about how long the device will keep working under abuse, which is why an american specifier writes grade 1 for a school corridor and accepts grade 2 for a back-of-house door that four people use a day. in the united states the fire-safety requirement itself comes from a separate document — nfpa 101 or the ibc — and the device also has to be listed for fire doors, usually by ul, if the opening is rated. en 1125 asks a different question entirely. it is the european standard for panic exit devices, and its subject is a crowd that does not know the building, in the dark, pushing. the test that defines it applies force to the bar and asks whether the door releases; the device must open with a single motion, from any point along the bar, without prior knowledge of how it works. that is why en 1125 devices are horizontal bars rather than knobs or levers — the standard is written around the behaviour of a body moving at speed, not around a hand. the distinction that catches buyers out is the one between en 1125 and en 179. both are european, both cover escape hardware, and they are not interchangeable. en 1125 is for panic situations: public buildings where the occupants are strangers to the layout — cinemas, shopping centres, schools, stadiums. en 179 is for emergency situations: buildings where the occupants know the exits, such as offices and staff-only areas, and where a lever handle or a push pad is acceptable because nobody will be pressing against the door in a crowd. specifying en 179 hardware on a public assembly door is a compliance failure even though the hardware is certified, because it is certified for the wrong situation. so the selection rule is short. if the project is in the united states, canada or a market that follows the american model, you need ansi/bhma a156.3 at the grade the specification calls for, plus a ul fire listing if the door is rated. if the project is in europe, the united kingdom, or one of the many markets — much of latin america, the gulf, parts of africa and asia — that have adopted the european standards, you need en 1125 for public buildings and en 179 where the occupants are familiar with the exits. nothing about the mechanism changes the answer; the country does. two practical consequences follow, and both cost money when they are missed. the first is that certification covers a tested assembly, not a shape. a device certified with a particular latch, a particular outside trim and particular fixings is certified in that combination; swapping the trim for a cheaper one, or fitting the bar with a strike it was not tested against, voids the claim even though every part looks the same. when you ask a supplier for a certificate, ask which model and which configuration it covers, and check the model number on the report against the model number on your order. the second is that the door matters as much as the device. a fire-rated opening is a rated assembly — leaf, frame, hinges, closer, seals and exit device together — and a certificate for the device alone says nothing about the assembly. on a double door, the sequence in which the two leaves close is part of that assembly, which is why a door coordinator is a safety component rather than an accessory. ordering two single-point devices for a pair of doors produces a pair that does not seal, and an inspector will fail it. where canton hyland stands, plainly. we manufacture push-bar exit devices — 42 models across fire-door, alarmed, multi-point, exterior-trim and special-application types — and we hold our own en 1125 test documentation, which we will supply against a named model for a tender. we do not hold ansi/bhma certification, and we say so rather than implying otherwise; a supplier who claims both for the same product without two sets of reports is claiming something no laboratory issued. if your project is american-specified, tell us at enquiry stage and we will tell you honestly whether we can serve it. if it is european-specified, ask for the report against the exact model you intend to buy, and read the model number twice. 001 023-et 027 301-s-s 309-d 310 316-d 320

title: The Door Schedule: How Hardware Is Actually Specified
subtitle: Insight
text: the door schedule: how hardware is actually specified projects do not buy locks. they buy door types, and each door type is a set of hardware that has to agree with itself. the document that decides this is the door schedule, and it is worth understanding before you quote against one. a manufacturer's catalogue is organised by product: lock cases here, lever handles there, closers somewhere else. a building is not organised that way. a building is a list of doors, and every door needs a set of hardware whose parts have to agree with each other — the same backset, the same handing, the same fire rating, the same finish. the document that records this is the door hardware schedule, and on a commercial project it is what the order is actually written from. if you sell into projects and have never seen one, this is roughly what a row looks like. a door type, say a fire-rated cross-corridor door leaf. its dimensions and handing. then a hardware set: a lock case with a stated backset and centre distance, a lever set on the plate that matches that centre distance, a euro cylinder keyed into the building's master system, a pair of hinges rated for the leaf weight, a closer with the right power size, and — because it is on an escape route — an exit device rather than a lock on the egress side. one row. seven line items. every one of them has to be compatible with the other six. two consequences follow, and they are the reason this document is worth understanding. the first is that a project buyer is never comparing your lock against a competitor's lock. they are comparing whether your lock fits the set. a case with an 85 mm centre distance and a 55 mm backset is either right for the plate and the door preparation already specified, or it is not, and no amount of quality argument moves that. this is why the dimensional questions arrive before the price questions, and why a supplier who answers them slowly loses the enquiry before quoting. the second is that hardware sets are where the quantities live. a schedule does not say two hundred locks. it says thirty of set hw-01, ninety of hw-02, and so on, and each set expands into its line items. a distributor pricing from a schedule needs the sets to expand cleanly into products they can order, which means a manufacturer who can supply the whole set is worth more than a cheaper one who supplies part of it — not because of loyalty, but because a split set means two lead times, two shipments and a coordination risk that lands on the distributor. the practical implication for anyone reading a schedule for the first time: read down the set, not across the catalogue. take one hardware set and satisfy every line in it before moving to the next. if a line cannot be matched, say so at that point rather than at quotation, because a set with a gap is more useful to the buyer as an early question than as a late surprise. there are three questions worth asking before you quote against a schedule at all. which sets are on escape routes, because those are governed by regulation rather than preference and the hardware is not interchangeable with the rest. whether there is a master key system, because if there is, the cylinders are a single coordinated order and not a per-door line item. and what the finish is across the project, because finish is usually specified once for the whole building and then repeated silently in every row. our catalogue is organised by product because that is how a catalogue has to be organised. but the enquiries that turn into orders almost never arrive product by product. they arrive as a schedule, or as a photograph of one, and the answer that wins is the one that reads the set rather than the line. if you have a schedule, send it — the useful reply is which sets we can complete, which we can complete except for one item, and which we cannot, and that reply is faster than a line-by-line quotation. 001 lc04 85*60 607 pbbk f100 ss

title: Backset and Centre Distance: How to Read a Mortise Lock Case Number
subtitle: Insight
text: backset and centre distance: how to read a mortise lock case number two numbers decide whether a lock case fits the door in front of you. they are printed in the model number, and getting them wrong is the most common reason a container of hardware cannot be installed. a distributor sends a purchase order for four hundred mortise lock cases. the model number is right, the finish is right, the price is agreed. eight weeks later the cases arrive on site, the installer offers one up to a prepared door, and the handle spindle sits fifteen millimetres from where the hole is. nothing is defective. the cases were simply made for a different door preparation, and the only clue was two digits in the model number that nobody read. this happens often enough that it is worth spelling out exactly what those digits mean, because once you can read them you can specify a lock case from its name alone. centre distance is the gap between the centre of the cylinder hole and the centre of the handle spindle, measured along the face of the lock. backset is the distance from the front edge of the faceplate back to the centre of that spindle. centre distance has to match the handle plate or escutcheon you are fitting. backset has to match how far in from the door edge the door was bored. they are independent of each other, and a lock case is only usable when both agree with the door. across the euro-profile range those two figures are the model number. lc08 85×55 is an 85 mm centre distance with a 55 mm backset. lc21 85×50 is the same 85 mm centre distance on a 50 mm backset. lc8520 compresses the same information without the separator: 85 mm centre distance, 20 mm backset. once you know the convention, a packing list becomes readable at a glance. eighty-five millimetres is the figure you will meet most often. it is the standard centre distance for euro-profile cylinder locks, and it is why a european handle plate drops onto a case from almost any manufacturer without drilling. seventy-two millimetres is the other one worth knowing — it is common through latin american markets, and it is why lc34 50×72 puts the backset first: at 72 mm centre distance the numbers read in the reverse order, so the model name follows the market's own convention rather than ours. backset is where the real variation lives, because backset follows the door rather than the standard. narrow aluminium stiles cannot take a deep case, so 16 mm, 17 mm and 20 mm backsets exist for them — that is what lc8520 at 20 mm and the 16 mm sliding-hook cases are for. timber doors take more, and 45 mm, 50 mm, 55 mm and 60 mm are the usual span. a 70 mm backset like the lc7065 puts the handle a long way in from the edge, which is what a wide entrance door with a heavy rail needs. two suffixes are worth recognising while you are reading the number. ps marks a passage case: latch only, no cylinder, for a door that closes but does not lock. and where the model carries a bolt count — lc04 85×60 and lc14 85×50 both run four round bolts alongside the latch — you are looking at a multi-point case meant for a security or entrance door rather than an interior one. the practical sequence when you specify is short. measure the door first, not the lock: how far in is the spindle hole bored, and what centre distance does the handle plate you intend to use require. then read those two figures out of the candidate model numbers. then confirm handing and faceplate dimensions, which the model number does not encode. if you are replacing existing hardware rather than fitting new doors, take the old case out and measure it — a door that was prepared once has already made both decisions for you, and matching it is cheaper than re-boring four hundred doors. where a dimension is not printed on our product pages, it is because we have not verified it for that model rather than because it does not matter. ask for the drawing before you order and we will send the one that covers the model on your schedule, or say plainly that it is still being prepared. lc08 85×55mm lc04 85*60 lc8520ps lc34 50×72mm lc7065

title: Why Aluminium Doors Drop, and What the Lock Case Has to Do With It
subtitle: Insight
text: why aluminium doors drop, and what the lock case has to do with it a narrow-stile aluminium door that no longer latches has almost never got a broken lock. it has dropped a few millimetres at the far edge, and the lock is simply the first place anyone notices. here is what actually moves, and which of it is a hardware decision. the complaint arrives in the same words every time: the lock has failed, the door will not latch, the key turns but the bolt misses the strike. in a narrow-stile aluminium door the lock is almost never the fault. the leaf has dropped — often by two or three millimetres at the lock edge — and the latch is now presenting itself below the hole it is supposed to enter. replacing the lock case fixes nothing, and it is the most common wasted purchase in this category. understand what a narrow stile is and the reason becomes obvious. the stile is the vertical member at the edge of the leaf, and on a commercial aluminium door it is often only 30 to 50mm wide, because the client wanted glass and not frame. that leaves a very small section of extruded aluminium to carry the entire weight of a large glazed leaf, resist the leverage of someone pulling on a handle a metre from the hinge, and house a lock cavity cut into the middle of it. the lock pocket removes material from the one part already doing the most work. three things move, in this order. the hinge or pivot side wears first, because every opening is a lever with the leaf as its arm — a 2.2 metre glazed door concentrates a great deal of moment onto a top pivot. second, the corner joints of the frame open slightly; a mitred aluminium corner held by cleats and screws is stiff but not infinitely so, and once it racks by a fraction of a degree the diagonal shortens and the free corner falls. third, and only third, the door furniture shows it — because the latch is a precision fit into a strike with perhaps 2mm of tolerance, and it is the first component in the assembly with no slack left to absorb the movement. this is why the hardware choice that matters most on a narrow-stile door is not the lock at all: it is what carries the leaf. a floor spring set into the slab takes the weight into the structure rather than into the frame corner, which is why a heavy glazed door on a floor spring stays square for years while the same leaf on butt hinges racks its frame. if you are specifying a door that is tall, wide, glazed, or used hundreds of times a day, the pivot decision is the anti-sag decision, and it has to be made before the floor is poured. now the part that genuinely is a lock-case decision. in a 30mm stile there is very little metal either side of the lock pocket, so the case has to be narrow, and its backset — the distance from the door edge to the centre of the follower — is fixed by the profile rather than chosen. our narrow-stile cases run at 30, 40 and 45mm backsets for exactly this reason; a 60mm backset case simply will not fit a narrow stile, and forcing a wider pocket into the extrusion removes the material the stile needs to stay stiff. ordering by backset first, and by everything else second, is the correct sequence for aluminium. two more details decide whether the installation survives. the first is latch throw. a door that has moved a millimetre still latches if the bolt is long enough to find the strike, and fails if it is not — which is why a hook bolt or a longer deadbolt throw is worth specifying on a wide leaf, and why our sliding hook-lock cases exist for aluminium sliders where a straight latch has nothing to bite. the second is the strike itself: an adjustable or slotted strike gives the installer a millimetre or two of vertical adjustment, and that is often the entire repair on a door that has dropped slightly. it costs almost nothing at order time and saves a site visit. so the checklist, in the order that prevents the problem rather than chases it. decide how the leaf is carried — floor spring for anything heavy, tall or glazed. measure the stile and pick the backset from it, not from a catalogue habit. choose a bolt with enough throw for the leaf width, and a hook rather than a latch on sliders. specify an adjustable strike. and when a door does drop, adjust the pivot and the strike before ordering anything: the lock case is the symptom, and replacing a symptom is how the same fault comes back next season. one honest note on what we publish. our lock cases carry backset, centre distance, case size and bolt throw on the product pages, because those are the numbers this decision turns on and several of them came off our own production drawings rather than out of marketing copy. what we do not yet publish is a load rating for the doors these cases suit — that depends on the leaf, the glazing and the pivot far more than on the lock, and a number invented for the lock alone would be worse than no number. send the leaf size, the stile width and the profile system, and the export team will tell you which backset fits and what to carry it on. ai8530 lc02 85-40 lc03 85-45 lc33 5572 lc7065 ju-071

title: Push Bar or Touch Bar: Which Panic Device Your Door Needs
subtitle: Insight
text: push bar or touch bar: which panic device your door needs a push bar pivots and travels; a touch bar depresses flush into its own housing. they cost differently, they fail differently, and only one of them survives a corridor that gets hit by trolleys. canton hyland builds the push-bar type across all 42 devices in the range. ask a supplier for a panic exit device and you will be offered two shapes without being told they are different products. one is a bar that stands off the door on two arms and swings toward the leaf when you push it. the other is a bar that sits almost flush in a full-width housing and sinks into that housing when you lean on it. the first is a push bar, sometimes called a crash bar or a panic bolt. the second is a touch bar, sometimes called a touch rail. every one of the 42 devices in the canton hyland range is the push-bar type. both do the same job in the same way as far as the law is concerned. a person moving at speed, in the dark, possibly carrying someone, hits the bar anywhere along its length and the door opens. neither requires a key, a code, or a second action, and that single-motion release is the whole point: en 1125 exists because doors that need two hands or a conscious decision have killed people in fires. what separates the two is not compliance. it is mechanism, and mechanism is what determines cost, wear and how the door behaves after five years of abuse. a push bar carries its load on two pivoting arms bolted through the door. when you push, the bar travels three or four centimetres toward the leaf and rotates those arms, which retract the latch. the travel is visible and the mechanism is exposed, which sounds like a disadvantage and is mostly the opposite: you can see what is worn, the moving parts are reachable without dismantling a housing, and a bent arm can be replaced on site. the exposed geometry is also why a push bar shrugs off the thing that destroys hardware in real buildings — a trolley, a bed, a pallet truck hitting the door at hip height. it hits the bar, the bar retracts, nothing binds. a touch bar hides its mechanism inside a housing that runs the full width of the door, and the bar depresses into that housing rather than travelling away from it. it looks better. on a hotel corridor or a gallery it looks considerably better, because there is no gap between bar and door collecting dust, and the profile is a clean horizontal line. the cost is that everything moving is inside a sealed extrusion. a distorted housing after an impact is not a part you swap; it is a device you replace. touch bars are also, as a class, more expensive to manufacture, which is why they dominate specification-led european projects and are rare on the price-sensitive end of the market. the choice usually makes itself from the building rather than from the door. a school corridor, a warehouse, a back-of-house route in a hotel, a hospital service door — anywhere carts move — takes a push bar, and takes it in stainless steel rather than a coated finish. a front-of-house fire exit in a building where the exit is visible to the public, and where nothing wider than a person passes through it, is where a touch bar earns its price. between those two cases sits most of the world, and most of the world buys push bars. two questions matter more than the bar shape and are asked less often. the first is what happens on the outside face. a panic device is an exit device: it guarantees you can get out, and says nothing about getting in. if the door is also an entrance, it needs outside trim — a lever, a knob or a pull, keyed or not — and that trim is a separate order line with its own finish and its own handing. our range carries exterior trim as its own sub-type for exactly this reason, because a device ordered without it arrives as a door that opens one way only, and that is discovered on site. the second is the double door. two leaves meeting in the middle need a decision about which leaf is active and what holds the inactive one shut. a device with top-and-bottom bolts — a multi-point or two-point locking version — pins the inactive leaf into the frame and the head, and the active leaf latches against it. ordering two single-point devices for a pair of doors produces a pair that rattles, does not seal against smoke, and will not pass an inspection. our multi-point and double-door versions exist as distinct models rather than as an option on the standard one. on certification, we will be plain, because this is where catalogues are least honest. panic hardware sold into europe is expected to carry en 1125, and a compliant device is a tested assembly — bar, latch, trim, fixings — not a shape. we hold our own test documentation and can supply it for a tender; ask the export team for the current report against the specific model you are quoting, and specify the model before the finish, because the finish never changes the test and the model always does. treat any datasheet quoting a standard number that does not exist as what it is. we have seen a competitor's page for a device in this category cite en 1205 compliance. there is no en 1205. it is a typo for en 1125 that has been copied from price list to price list for years, and it tells you how much of this industry's paperwork is transcription rather than testing. 001 015 023-et 027 301-s-s 310 316-d

title: What the Letters After a Model Number Mean
subtitle: Insight
text: what the letters after a model number mean 607 pb, 607 ab, 607 sn and 607 bn are the same lock in four finishes. the letters are a finish code and a function code, read from the right, and once you can read them a price list of four hundred lines collapses into about sixty products. open any chinese hardware manufacturer's price list and you will find the same thing: four hundred lines that look like four hundred products, and are not. somewhere in there are 607 pbbk, 607 abet, 607 snet and 607 bnet, and a buyer new to the catalogue reasonably assumes these are four different locks that happen to share a number. they are one lock. the digits are the product. the letters are the finish, and sometimes the function. nobody writes this down, because inside a factory it is too obvious to explain and outside one there is no way to find out. so here it is written down. the finish codes are two letters, and most of the set runs across the whole industry rather than being ours alone. pb is polished brass. ab is antique brass. ac is antique copper. sn is satin nickel. sc is satin chrome. cp is chrome plated. sb is satin brass. sp is bright polished. bn is black nickel. ss is stainless steel, and where a supplier distinguishes the two grades of it, sss is satin stainless and pss is polished stainless. two more are sprayed coatings rather than platings: w and wl are white paint, and f is a wood-grain spray. our own price list spells several of these out in its finish column — pb=polish brass on the 6094, sn=satin nickel on the 70710, sc=satin chrome on the 70610, bn black nickle on the 9211 — and once you have seen the pattern once, the rest of the list reads itself. a second group of letters is the function rather than the finish. et is the entrance function, keyed from the outside. ps is passage: latch only, no cylinder, for a door that closes but never locks. bk is the privacy or bathroom function, with a turn button inside and an emergency release outside. so 607 pbbk is a 607 in polished brass, privacy function; 607 snet is the same lock in satin nickel, keyed entrance. read the letters from the right: the function comes last, the finish sits in front of it. 592 sset is ss plus et — stainless steel, entrance — not s plus set, which is why reading left to right gets this backwards. this matters commercially in a way that is easy to miss. a distributor who reads the codes stops quoting four hundred products and starts quoting sixty, each in the finishes their market actually buys. it shortens the range, shortens the conversation, and shortens the sample order — because a sample of the mechanism in one finish tells you what the other five feel like. it also changes what you check before ordering. if the letters are the finish, then the finish is the part of the order most easily got wrong, and the part a photograph settles fastest. ask for the finish you intend to order rather than accepting the one that happens to be photographed, and if a supplier sends the polished brass image against an antique copper line, treat that as a question rather than a detail. one honest caveat about our own list. where the finish column reads ab/ac/pb/sb/ss/sp/sc all available, that is the range the model can be produced in, not the finish of the piece in the photograph. a range in a specification is not a specification, and the two are worth keeping apart in your own records. a handful of older lines also carry a letter we have not confirmed the meaning of — s, e, d and a few others — and where we are not certain, our product pages say nothing rather than guessing. if you are building a purchase order from a list like this, the useful sequence is: identify the mechanism from the digits, choose the function from the third letter group, then choose the finish last and confirm it in writing against a photograph of that exact code. the first two decisions are engineering. the last one is the one that arrives in a container and either matches the door or does not. 607 pbbk 6094 pbbk 70710 sn 70610 sc

title: 304, 201 or 316: Which Stainless Steel You Are Actually Buying
subtitle: Insight
text: 304, 201 or 316: which stainless steel you are actually buying three grades look identical in a photograph, cost very differently, and behave nothing alike within sight of the sea. 201 substitutes manganese for nickel and rusts where 304 does not; 316 adds molybdenum and survives where 304 pits. here is how to tell which one you have been quoted. a stainless handle costs anywhere between four and eleven dollars from chinese factories that are all photographing the same shape against the same white background. the photographs are not lying. the metal is different, and the difference does not appear until the hardware has been on a building for a year — which is long after the container cleared, the retention was released and the buyer moved on. there are three grades in ordinary circulation. 304 is the default architectural stainless: roughly 18% chromium, 8% nickel, no deliberate molybdenum. it is what most people mean when they say stainless steel, it is what most specifications intend, and in a normal inland building it does not corrode. 201 is a substitution alloy invented when nickel got expensive — it drops the nickel to around 4% and makes up the austenite with manganese and nitrogen. it is cheaper by a fifth to a third, it polishes to a finish indistinguishable from 304 across a showroom, and it carries noticeably less corrosion resistance. 316 goes the other way, adding 2 to 3% molybdenum specifically to resist chloride attack, which is the failure mode that pits 304 near salt water and in swimming pools. the practical consequence is narrow and sharp. inland, in a dry or temperate climate, 201 will very often be fine for the life of the fit-out, which is why it exists and why it is not a scam. within a few kilometres of the sea, in a coastal hotel, on a pool enclosure, or anywhere the air carries chloride, 201 develops rust freckles in a single season and 304 develops them eventually. that is the specific case where 316 stops being an upgrade and starts being the only correct answer. it is also the case that produces the most warranty arguments in this industry, because the hardware did not fail — it was the wrong grade for the exposure, and nobody wrote the exposure down. you can narrow it down on a sample without a laboratory, provided you know what the test does and does not prove. take a magnet to it. properly annealed 304 is essentially non-magnetic, and a fridge magnet slides off; 201 is usually weakly magnetic and the magnet drags or tugs. this is a useful screen and it is not proof: cold working — the stamping and forming that makes a rose or a plate — induces magnetism in 304 too, so a magnetic edge on a pressed part means nothing on its own. test the flat, unformed area, compare against a sample you trust, and treat a strong pull as a reason to ask rather than a verdict. if the answer matters commercially, the only thing that settles it is a material certificate or a positive material identification test on the delivered goods, and both are things you are entitled to ask for before you place the order rather than after. two more things travel under the same word and are not grades at all. the first is finish: sss is satin stainless, pss is polished stainless, and both codes describe the surface treatment, not the alloy underneath. a polished 201 handle and a polished 304 handle carry the same finish code. the second is construction. a great deal of hardware sold as stainless is stainless-clad or stainless-plated over zinc alloy or steel, which behaves like the substrate as soon as the skin is scratched. if a lever is priced far below the others in a comparison, the interesting question is usually not the grade but whether it is solid at all. we will be direct about our own catalogue, because the audit that prompted this article was of our own data. of the 165 canton hyland records whose material field mentions stainless steel, 21 state a grade explicitly — some as 304, some as 201, several as "304/201" where the model is genuinely offered in both. the remaining records say "stainless steel" and stop. that is a gap in our published data, not a gap in the factory: the grade is known at production and is confirmed on request against a specific model and order quantity. we are filling it in as the records are revised, and in the meantime the honest instruction is to ask, and to get the answer in writing on the proforma rather than in a chat message. the question to send a supplier is not "is this stainless steel?", because the answer is always yes and it settles nothing. ask three things in one line: which grade, solid or plated, and will you state it on the invoice. a supplier who answers all three specifically is quoting you a real product. a supplier who answers "high quality stainless" is quoting you a photograph. one last note on where grade genuinely does not matter. interior door furniture in a dry building — a bathroom hook in a private house, an indicator on an office door, a hinge in a corridor — is not an environment that distinguishes these alloys within any reasonable service life. specifying 316 there is money spent on a certificate. the grade conversation is worth having on external doors, coastal and marine projects, pool and spa areas, commercial kitchens and anywhere cleaning is done with chloride-based products. everywhere else, buy 304 and spend the difference on the lock. lh1033 ss lh1016 ncb 301-s-s gl125 ss

title: What One Frameless Glass Door Actually Needs
subtitle: Insight
text: what one frameless glass door actually needs a frameless glass door is not a product, it is an assembly of six or seven parts ordered from three different categories. buyers quote the handle, forget the floor spring, and discover the over-panel patch on site. here is the whole list, in the order it gets forgotten. nobody sells a frameless glass door. what gets sold is a sheet of toughened glass with holes and notches cut into it before tempering, plus six or seven separate metal parts that clamp to it. the glass comes from a local processor. the metal comes from us. the part nobody remembers to order is almost always the same one, and it is not the handle. start at the bottom, because that is where the door's weight and its entire closing behaviour live. a frameless door pivots on a floor spring — a hydraulic body set into the finished floor in a cement box, carrying the leaf's weight and controlling how fast it swings back. it is the most expensive single item on the list, it is the one with the longest lead time, and it has to be ordered before the floor screed is poured, because retrofitting one means cutting up a finished floor. our ju-series floor springs sit in the door-closers category rather than under glass, which is a catalogue convention rather than a hint about what they are for, and it is a common reason a glass-door quote comes back missing its most important line. the floor spring does not touch the glass directly. a bottom patch fitting clamps to the lower corner of the leaf and engages the spring's spindle, transferring the load. at the top, a matching top patch fitting takes a pivot pin. those two are the minimum, and they are handed as a pair for a single door — which means a pair of doors needs two sets, mirrored, and ordering four identical patches gets you two doors that both open the wrong way. above the door, if the opening is taller than the leaf, there is a fixed glass over-panel, and the joint between door and over-panel takes an over-panel patch — a connector that clamps both sheets and carries the top pivot. this is the part that gets discovered on site. a buyer measures the door, orders top and bottom patches, and finds on installation day that the top patch has nothing to fix to, because the head of the opening is glass rather than structure. if there is glass above the door, there is a third patch in the order. then the lock, and here the sequence matters more than the part. a glass door lock is a patch-style body clamped to the leaf, engaging either a floor socket or a strike in the adjacent panel. both the lock body and its counterpart need cut-outs in the glass, and toughened glass cannot be cut, drilled or notched after tempering. every hole, every notch, every corner cut-out has to be on the processor's drawing before the sheet goes in the furnace. deciding to add a lock after the glass is made means buying the glass again. this is the single most expensive mistake on a frameless job and it is always a sequencing mistake, never a hardware one. last, the pull handle, which is the part everyone starts with. ours run from 300mm to 600mm in the 100-series, in back-to-back and single-sided arrangements, and the number that matters is not the overall length but the fixing centre — the distance between the two holes, because the holes are in the glass and the glass is already made. our published centre distances come off the production drawings rather than off marketing copy, and they differ between models that look identical: 148mm on the 100 and the 107, 147mm on the 102, 125mm on the 106. a millimetre is not a rounding error when the hole is already drilled. so the checklist for one door, in the order things go wrong: floor spring, bottom patch, top patch, over-panel patch if there is glass above, lock body, floor socket or strike, pull handle. then two numbers that govern all of them — the glass thickness, because patch fittings are made for a specific range and 10mm and 12mm are not interchangeable, and the fixing centre on the handle. our patch range is built for 10 to 12mm toughened glass; confirm the thickness with the processor before the fittings are ordered, not after. one thing we do not currently publish, and should: which of our patch fittings, locks and floor springs are designed to work together as a set. we make all three, the combinations are known in the factory, and a buyer cannot see them from the catalogue — the parts sit in three different categories and nothing joins them up. until that is fixed on the site, send the export team the leaf size, the glass thickness, whether there is an over-panel and whether the door needs to lock, and ask for the parts list rather than for a price on a handle. it takes one email and it prevents the two failures above, both of which cost more than the hardware. f101 f110 f112 gl125 ss 100 107 ju-071
